title: Breathless After a Cold, Clamshell Scar / Infection and Rejection Look Alike

blocks.text: Breathless After a Cold, Clamshell Scar / Infection and Rejection Look Alike

AMaC MRCP PACES · R2-01 · Physical examination · PACES Station 1, respiratory examination · Skills A, B, D, E, G · 10 minutes (up to 6 minutes examining, then at least 4 minutes of examiner questions) · Guidelines: ISHLT consensus report: Chronic lung allograft dysfunction (2019); ISHLT consensus document for the selection of lung transplant candidates (2021) · Related AMaC: AMaC cystic fibrosis and bronchiectasis examination stations; this one tests the transplant and infection versus rejection
Ms Bethan Rowlands is 34 and works as a teaching assistant. She has had ten days of increasing breathlessness after a cold. Please examine her respiratory system to establish the cause.
You may examine for up to 6 minutes. The examiners will then ask you questions.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. A clamshell scar means a transplant, and a breathless transplant patient has infection or rejection: they look alike at the bedside, so name both and bring in the transplant centre today.

The Examiner Trap. Candidates see the scar, say "transplant" and stop, or call it a chest infection. Pass: find the immunosuppression signs, infer the original disease, and name infection and rejection together. Fail: oral antibiotics, home, and a higher steroid dose.

rows: Think
Say
Do
She is immunosuppressed and breathless: clean hands first, then position and consent.
"May I examine your chest? Does anything hurt, and is your scar tender?"
Clean hands; introduce, consent; sit her at 45 degrees; look at the hands, face and chest wall before touching.
Look for the scar, the drug effects and clues to the first disease, then compare both sides.
"I'm going to tap and listen on both sides, from the back, and ask you to say 'ninety-nine'."
Hands, tremor, bruising, face, mouth; chest wall; expansion, percussion, breath sounds; nodes; legs; cover her; clean hands.
Say what she has, what could be wrong now, and why you cannot separate them here.
"This is a bilateral lung transplant, probably for cystic fibrosis. Infection and rejection both fit, so I'd involve the transplant team today."
Present in order; original disease; differential; investigations; same-day transplant centre contact; thank her.

Welfare and infection safety
Starts without cleaning hands or consent; presses the scar roughly; leaves her exposed.
Cleans hands, introduces self, consents, asks about pain and scar tenderness, sits her at 45 degrees, covers her, cleans hands again.
Also offers a chaperone, keeps exposure to the minimum, and pauses if she tires.
R2
A
Systematic technique
Disorganised; omits the hands, face or chest wall, or examines one side only.
Hands, face, mouth and chest wall, then expansion, percussion and auscultation from the back, comparing sides.
Also checks the neck and axillary nodes and the legs.
R3
B
Identifying signs
Misses the scar or tremor, or reports a dull base or bronchial breathing that is not present.
Finds the clamshell scar, fine tremor, thin bruised forearm skin and fine bibasal crackles.
Also finds the port scar and facial rounding, and states no dullness, wheeze or bronchial breathing.
R4
D
Differential diagnosis
Calls it a simple chest infection, or names rejection only.
Bilateral lung transplant, probably for cystic fibrosis, with infection or rejection as the cause now.
Also lists viral, fungal and bacterial infection, chronic allograft dysfunction and drug toxicity, with reasons.
R5
E
Investigations
Chest X-ray and antibiotics only; no cultures or bronchoscopy.
Spirometry against her baseline, chest imaging, sputum and viral tests, immunosuppressant drug levels, and bronchoscopy with biopsy through the transplant centre.
Also says infection must be excluded before rejection is treated, and why.
R6
E
Management
Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): changes steroids or immunosuppression alone, or sends her home without contacting the transplant centre.
Treats her as unwell, contacts the transplant centre today, and changes no immunosuppression without them.
Also asks the pharmacist to check drug interactions and arranges admission with infection precautions.

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail.
Not used for this station type.

Findings, released as each step is done: inspection: thin, mildly breathless at rest; respiratory rate 22; pulse 104 regular; blood pressure 118/72; SpO2 93% on air; temperature 37.8 °C. Hands: no clubbing; fine postural tremor; thin, bruised forearm skin; no skin lesions. Face: mild rounding; no thrush. Chest wall: healed transverse scar across the lower chest below the breasts; healed port scar, right upper chest. Trachea central; no nodes. Expansion symmetrical, mildly reduced; percussion resonant; breath sounds vesicular; fine inspiratory crackles at both bases; no wheeze. No leg oedema; calves soft.

Question ladder: 1. What do you see? (B) Bilateral transplant, probably cystic fibrosis. 2. Why is she breathless now? (D) Infection, rejection, chronic lung allograft dysfunction (only with a persistent fall in FEV1 once other causes are excluded), drugs, oedema, clot. 3. Can you tell infection from rejection here? (D) No. 4. Investigations? (E) As the grid. 5. Management? (E) Transplant centre today; no immunosuppression change alone.

Curveballs: Drug level high: kidney and drug-interaction check with the pharmacist. A new forearm lesion: urgent suspected skin cancer referral. More breathless: sit upright, call senior help, oxygen per local protocol.
Cleans hands, introduces self, gains consent and asks about scar pain (G)
Inspects hands, face and chest wall before touching (A)
Finds the clamshell scar and says what it means (B)
Reports tremor and thin bruised skin as drug clues (B)
Compares both sides for expansion, percussion and breath sounds (A)
States no wheeze, dullness or bronchial breathing rather than inventing signs (B)
Names the transplant and the likely original disease from the clues (D)
Names infection and rejection together and says they cannot be separated here (D)
Plans bronchoscopy and drug levels, with infection excluded first (E)
Contacts the transplant centre today and changes nothing alone (E)
Covers her, cleans hands again and thanks her (G)
Fail performance
CANDIDATE: Sit back. [R1 Fail]
CANDIDATE: (Listens at the front of the chest, does not look at the scar.) [R2 Fail] [R3 Fail] It's a chest infection. [R4 Fail]
EXAMINER: Plan?
CANDIDATE: Chest X-ray and oral antibiotics. [R5 Fail] Send her home and increase her steroids if she is no better. [R6 Fail]

Examiner note: Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): steroids increased without excluding infection and no contact with the transplant centre. Hands were not cleaned, the scar and drug signs were missed, only the front was examined, and the diagnosis ignored the transplant.
Pass performance
CANDIDATE: (Cleans hands.) Ms Rowlands, I'm one of the doctors. May I examine your chest? Does anything hurt, and is the scar tender? Is this angle comfortable? [R1 Pass]
CANDIDATE: (Hands, face, mouth and chest wall; expansion, percussion and auscultation from the back, comparing sides.) [R2 Pass]
CANDIDATE: She has a fine tremor, thin bruised forearm skin, a healed transverse scar across the lower chest, and fine bibasal crackles. [R3 Pass]
CANDIDATE: (Covers her, cleans hands.) Thank you. [R1 Pass]
EXAMINER: Diagnosis?
CANDIDATE: A bilateral lung transplant, probably for cystic fibrosis, now with infection or rejection. [R4 Pass]
EXAMINER: Investigations?
CANDIDATE: Spirometry against her baseline, chest imaging, sputum and viral tests, drug levels, and bronchoscopy with biopsy through the transplant centre. [R5 Pass]
EXAMINER: Management?
CANDIDATE: Treat her as unwell, contact the transplant centre today, and change no immunosuppression without them. [R6 Pass]
Examiner note: Clean, safe and complete: found the scar and drug signs, named both causes and involved the transplant centre. Did not give the wider differential or state the negatives.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: (Cleans hands.) Ms Rowlands, I'm one of the doctors. May I examine your chest? Would you like a chaperone? I'll keep you covered and stop if you tire. [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: (Hands, face, chest wall; both sides from the back; neck and axillary nodes; legs.) [R2 High]
CANDIDATE: There is a clamshell scar and a healed port scar, tremor, bruising and facial rounding. No dullness, wheeze or bronchial breathing; fine bibasal crackles. [R3 High]
EXAMINER: Diagnosis?

CANDIDATE: Bilateral transplant, probably for cystic fibrosis. Now bacterial, viral or fungal infection, rejection, chronic allograft dysfunction, drug toxicity or oedema. I cannot separate them here. [R4 High]
EXAMINER: Investigations?
CANDIDATE: Infection must be excluded before rejection is treated, so sputum, viral tests and bronchoscopy with lavage and biopsy, plus drug levels and spirometry. [R5 High]
EXAMINER: Management?
CANDIDATE: Admit with infection precautions, call the transplant centre today, and ask the pharmacist to check interactions. [R6 High]
Examiner note: Added a chaperone offer, nodes and legs, the port scar, the full differential and the reason infection comes first, and pharmacy input. Anticipated each question.
R1: Not cleaning hands. She is immunosuppressed, so the examiner sees a candidate who could carry infection to her and who has ignored her welfare.
R3: Missing the clamshell scar. The transplant is never recognised, so every later answer addresses the wrong patient.
R4: Calling it a chest infection. Rejection and the transplant are left out, and the plan stops at antibiotics.
R5: Chest X-ray and antibiotics only. The cause is never established and rejection or chronic allograft dysfunction is missed.
R6: Raising steroids alone. Untreated infection can worsen under more immunosuppression, and the transplant centre is not told.
"Let me look at her chest wall again before I go on."
"I can't separate infection from rejection at the bedside, so I would involve the transplant team."
"May I summarise what I have found and give my diagnosis?"
Clamshell scar: bilateral transplant. A healed port scar and low weight suggest cystic fibrosis, a recognised indication for bilateral lung transplant (ISHLT 2021).
Immunosuppressants: a calcineurin inhibitor causes tremor, kidney injury and high blood pressure; steroids cause bruising and thin skin; all raise infection and skin cancer risk.

Chronic lung allograft dysfunction (CLAD) is a persistent fall in FEV1 of 20% or more from post-transplant baseline: probable CLAD once confirmed at least 3 weeks apart, definite once persisting 3 months (ISHLT 2019). An acute ten-day deterioration alone does not establish CLAD.
THINK: Infection or rejection; she is immunosuppressed.
SAY: "Bilateral lung transplant, probably for cystic fibrosis."
DO: Clean hands; read the scar and hands; compare both sides.

NUMBERS: Chronic allograft dysfunction: FEV1 down 20% or more from baseline; probable CLAD once confirmed at least 3 weeks apart, definite once persisting 3 months (ISHLT 2019). Scenario: SpO2 93%, temperature 37.8 °C.
TRAP: Calling it a chest infection.
FINISH: Transplant centre today; bronchoscopy; no steroid change alone.

Verleden GM et al. Chronic lung allograft dysfunction: definition, diagnostic criteria, and approaches to treatment. ISHLT consensus report. J Heart Lung Transplant 2019;38(5). https://ishlt.org/education-and-publications/standards-guidelines-detail/chronic-lung-allograft-dysfunction-definition-diagnostic-criteria-and-approaches-to-treatment Supports: Definition (persistent FEV1 fall of 20% or more from baseline; probable CLAD once confirmed at least 3 weeks apart, definite once persisting 3 months) and exclusion of infection and acute rejection.
